claims.statement: BEIR comprises 18 English zero-shot evaluation datasets from 9 retrieval tasks, with corpus sizes from 3.6k to 15M documents, average query lengths of 3 to 192 words and average document lengths of 11 to 635 words.
claims.scope: the benchmark as released; MS MARCO reported but outside the 18 zero-shot datasets
confidence_reasons: descriptive counts from the authors' Table 1 and text

claims.statement: The authors describe two earlier retrieval benchmarks as narrow: MultiReQA covers one task (question answering; five of eight datasets from Wikipedia; six of eight with fewer than 100k candidate sentences) and KILT retrieves only from Wikipedia and treats retrieval as a secondary task.
claims.scope: as characterized by the BEIR authors; the cited works themselves were not read

claims.statement: All datasets are scored with nDCG@10, computed with the Python interface of the official TREC evaluation tool; the authors chose it because Precision and Recall are rank-unaware and MRR and MAP cannot handle graded relevance.
claims.scope: all reported scores

claims.statement: Ten systems from five families (lexical: BM25; sparse: DeepCT, SPARTA, docT5query; dense: DPR, ANCE, TAS-B, GenQ; late-interaction: ColBERT; re-ranking: BM25+CE) were evaluated from public pre-trained checkpoints, with neural models reading only the first 512 word pieces of each document.
claims.scope: the ten configurations described

claims.statement: On in-domain MS MARCO, BM25 (nDCG@10 0.228) scored 7 to 18 points below the neural approaches trained on it, yet on the zero-shot datasets the summary row places DeepCT at - 27.9%, SPARTA - 20.3%, DPR - 47.7%, ANCE - 7.4%, TAS-B - 2.8% and GenQ - 3.6% relative to BM25.
claims.scope: nDCG@10; 18 zero-shot datasets; single evaluations

claims.statement: In this comparison, in-domain performance did not predict zero-shot performance: many approaches that outperform BM25 in-domain performed poorly on the BEIR datasets, and models fine-tuned with identical training data generalized differently.
claims.scope: the ten systems, MS MARCO training, the 18 datasets
confidence_reasons: consistent across DeepCT, SPARTA, ANCE, TAS-B
permitted_verbs: did not predict in this comparison

claims.statement: Averaged over the zero-shot datasets, BM25+CE was + 11% relative to BM25, ColBERT + 2.5% and docT5query + 1.6%; BM25+CE outperformed BM25 on 16 of 18 datasets, docT5query on 11 of 18 and ColBERT on 9 of 18.
claims.scope: nDCG@10; 18 zero-shot datasets

claims.statement: BM25+CE did not outperform BM25 on ArguAna (0.311 vs 0.315) or Touche-2020 (0.271 vs 0.367), which the authors describe as tasks extremely different from the MS MARCO training data; DeepCT and SPARTA underperformed BM25 on nearly all zero-shot datasets.
claims.scope: nDCG@10

claims.statement: Among dense models TAS-B outperformed ANCE on 14 of 18 datasets and DPR on 17 of 18; DPR, the only model not trained on MS MARCO, generalized worst; dense models underperformed BM25 on datasets with large domain shift (BioASQ) or task shift (Touche-2020).
claims.scope: nDCG@10; the three public dense checkpoints
confidence_reasons: checkpoints differ in training data and backbone

claims.statement: GenQ, which fine-tunes TAS-B on synthetic queries for each target corpus, outperformed TAS-B on specialized domains (scientific publications, finance, StackExchange; e.g. TREC-COVID 0.619 vs 0.481) and was weaker on Wikipedia-based datasets (e.g. NQ 0.358 vs 0.463); the pattern is not uniform (SCIDOCS 0.143 vs 0.149).
claims.scope: nDCG@10; GenQ corpora capped at 100K documents

claims.statement: TAS-B scored 17.3 points below ANCE on TREC-COVID and 7.8 points below on Touche-2020; the median length of their top-10 retrieved documents was 10 words versus 160 (TREC-COVID) and 14 versus 89 (Touche-2020).
claims.scope: two datasets
permitted_verbs: retrieved documents with a median length of

claims.statement: In a controlled comparison of two distilbert-base-uncased models trained identically on MS MARCO except for the similarity function, nDCG@10 (cosine vs dot-product) was 0.482 vs 0.635 on TREC-COVID, 0.261 vs 0.243 on Signal-1M and 0.670 vs 0.685 on FEVER, and the cosine model retrieved shorter documents on all datasets. Differences computed from the table: +15.3, -1.8 and +1.5 points for dot-product versus cosine.
claims.scope: one model pair; three datasets tabulated

claims.statement: The length preference of TAS-B versus ANCE may be related to the training loss or the similarity function; the controlled experiment shows a similarity function alone can change retrieved length, but TAS-B and ANCE also differ in backbone, loss and negative mining, so the source of their difference is not isolated.
claims.scope: TAS-B vs ANCE on TREC-COVID and Touche-2020
confidence_reasons: no ablation on the released systems

claims.statement: The good zero-shot performance of BM25+CE and ColBERT suggests that cross-attention and cross-attention-like operations matter for out-of-distribution generalization.
claims.scope: the ten systems

claims.statement: The authors speculate that TAS-B's stronger generalization among dense models comes from its training setup (in-batch negatives with Margin-MSE and strong ensemble teachers in knowledge distillation); this is untested.
claims.scope: TAS-B

claims.statement: On 1M sampled DBPedia documents, re-ranking (BM25+CE) and late interaction (ColBERT) were the slowest (> 350 ms), dense retrievers were 20-30x faster (< 20ms), and on CPU sparse models took 20-25ms; index sizes were 0.4GB for BM25, docT5query, DeepCT and BM25+CE, 3GB for dense models, 12GB for SPARTA and 20GB for ColBERT, and for BioASQ (~15M documents) ColBERT needs ~900GB versus 18GB for BM25.
claims.scope: 1M-document DBPedia subsample; stated CPU and GPU; exact search for dense, ANN for ColBERT

claims.statement: On TREC-COVID the share of top-10 hits never judged by annotators (Hole@10) was 6.4% for BM25, 2.8% for docT5query, 1.6% for BM25+CE, 14.4% for ANCE, 31.8% for TAS-B and 30.6% for DPR.
claims.scope: TREC-COVID, 50 queries

claims.statement: After the authors annotated the 980 unjudged query-document pairs, lexical systems changed little (docT5query 0.713 to 0.714; BM25 0.656 to 0.668), whereas ANCE rose from 0.654 to 0.735 (6.7 points above BM25), ColBERT from 0.677 to 0.735 (5.8 points), DPR from 0.332 to 0.445 and TAS-B from 0.481 to 0.555. Differences computed from these values: TAS-B +7.4 points, DPR +11.3 points, BM25+CE +0.3 points.
claims.scope: TREC-COVID nDCG@10; annotators blind to the system

claims.statement: These results indicate that the TREC-COVID annotation pool, although built from many participating systems, favours lexical approaches; the authors argue the same lexical-bias mechanism applies to datasets such as BioASQ and Signal-1M, which was not measured there.
claims.scope: measured only on TREC-COVID
confidence_reasons: direct manipulation of missing labels on one dataset
extension to other datasets rests on descriptions of how they were built

claims.statement: The authors observe low weighted-Jaccard word overlap between datasets from different domains and read it as evidence that BEIR requires generalization to diverse domains.
claims.scope: unigram word overlap only
confidence_reasons: soft evidence; figure values not extracted
word overlap is a proxy for domain difference

claims.statement: BEIR is released as a pip-installable Python package with wrappers for several retrieval toolkits, a standard data format (corpus, queries, qrels) and an actively maintained leaderboard; the repository README lists preprocessed datasets and marks four (BioASQ, Signal-1M, TREC-NEWS, Robust04) as not directly downloadable, with reproduction instructions.
claims.scope: as documented in the paper and README

claims.statement: A later publication listed in the repository README (Kamalloo et al., 2024) provides reproducible reference implementations for learned dense and sparse models and meta-analyses of effect sizes across BEIR datasets, motivated by the difficulty of interpreting a single average over heterogeneous datasets.
claims.scope: as stated in its abstract reproduced in the README

claims.statement: Better datasets built with diverse pooling strategies are needed for fair comparison of retrieval approaches, and BEIR's integration of many systems makes creating such diverse pools simpler; multilingual, long-document, multi-factor and multi-field tasks are left for future work.
claims.scope: future work as stated by the authors

claims.statement: No single system was best on every dataset; the two systems with the highest zero-shot averages (BM25+CE and ColBERT) were the slowest and, for ColBERT, the largest index, docT5query (the third system above BM25) had a BM25-sized index of 0.4GB, and the cheaper dense and sparse retrievers often averaged below BM25, which remained a strong zero-shot baseline in this comparison.
claims.scope: the ten systems, the 18 datasets, nDCG@10, one efficiency setup

limitations.statement: All 18 datasets are English; multilingual and cross-lingual retrieval are not covered.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Rankings of systems may not carry over to other languages.

limitations.statement: Long-document retrieval is not covered, and neural models read only the first 512 word pieces of each document.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Results for neural models on long documents (e.g. Robust04 with 466.40-word average) reflect truncated input.
limitations.resolution: A different setup would be needed.

limitations.statement: Only pure text search over one or two fields is evaluated; no PageRank, recency, click-through or multi-field signals.
Task-specific models are not evaluated; the benchmark targets models that generalize.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Conclusions about which architectures are best do not apply to specialist systems.

limitations.statement: Each system was evaluated once from public checkpoints; no seeds, variance or confidence intervals are reported, and no significance tests are run.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Small differences (for example 0.643 vs 0.644 on SciFact) cannot be judged as real; only larger and consistent patterns are interpreted.
limitations.resolution: Repeated training or bootstrap over queries.

limitations.statement: The annotation-bias analysis covers only TREC-COVID and only the systems evaluated; the authors themselves annotated the missing pairs and report no agreement statistics.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The extent of lexical bias in other datasets is not measured.

limitations.statement: Efficiency was measured on one 1M-document DBPedia sample, on one CPU and one GPU type; dense models use exact search and ColBERT approximate search.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Latency ratios may differ at other scales or with approximate indexes for dense models.

limitations.statement: The compared systems differ in more than architecture (backbone, training data, negative mining, corpus caps for GenQ at 100K documents, a re-implemented SPARTA), and total compute is not reported.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Family-level conclusions are conclusions about these particular checkpoints.

limitations.statement: The summary 'Avg. Performance vs. BM25' aggregates heterogeneous datasets into one number whose formula is not defined in the paper text; per-dataset results are the primary evidence.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Rankings by average should be read with the per-dataset counts.

limitations.statement: Mechanistic explanations (cross-attention, TAS-B training loss, length preference) are not tested by ablation on the released systems.
Cited works were not read in full; descriptions of them come from the project's own text, and the diversity analysis rests on unigram overlap.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Related-work statements are attributions, not independent checks.

limitations.statement: Only three datasets of the cosine versus dot-product comparison are available in the extracted table; the text says dot-product was worse on a majority of other datasets.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The size of the effect on other datasets is not reported here.
